claims.text: The baseline is a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy thin coating deposited by laser cladding on a conventional metal substrate.
Standard laser-cladding parameters produce a baseline coating with minimal intrinsic residual stress.
Increasing laser power while adjusting deposition speed will introduce compressive residual stress into the coating.
A brief post-deposition tempering step will stabilize the induced compressive stress against relaxation at high temperature.
The modified coating will contain a stabilized residual compressive-stress field during high-temperature sliding.
Residual compressive stress raises the activation-energy barrier for dislocation nucleation.
Residual compressive stress inhibits dislocation propagation or motion.
Inhibiting dislocation nucleation and motion delays microcrack formation.
The engineered compressive-stress field suppresses localized microscopic deformation patterns.
Suppressing localized deformation produces more homogeneous plastic flow during sliding.
More homogeneous plastic flow reduces coating wear.
The stress-stabilized coating will have a lower wear rate than the minimal-residual-stress baseline.
The stress-stabilized coating will exhibit a more diffuse and homogeneous microscopic deformation pattern than the baseline.
The predicted wear and deformation effects should hold during sliding at 300–500 °C in an inert or controlled atmosphere.
Using an inert atmosphere minimizes oxidation effects during the high-temperature wear test.
Prolonged high-temperature exposure may significantly relax the engineered compressive stress despite tempering.
Relaxation of the compressive stress would diminish its beneficial wear and deformation effects.
Residual-stress profiles can be measured using X-ray or neutron diffraction.
Coating wear rate can be quantified through mass loss or volume loss.
Failure to obtain both a statistically significant wear-rate reduction and less-localized deformation relative to the baseline would falsify the hypothesis.
